#5445. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5444. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5443. ‘The best thing that you can do for your career is to make yourself redundant’: Inside Stellantis’ AI push after the ‘starting gun went off’

The Grand Cherokee is lined with wood paneling, its windshield is cracked, and chunks are cut out of its side-view mirrors like pierced ears. That’s where the cameras go, a grinning Joydip Saha tells me from behind the wheel. The manager of Stellantis’ hands-free driving project lovingly taps what he calls “the most broken-up car,” jerry-rigged with a yellow box sitting on the dashboard that lets a human grab control. It’s an industry-standard “kill switch” used in many prototype vehicles. In technical terms, the safety driver can hit the kill switch to disconnect power to the advanced driver assist system module, stopping the ADAS system from controlling the vehicle. Then, the driver has full control over the vehicle.

Another piece of equipment connected to the kill switch — the STLA AutoDrive L2++ system embedded in the vehicle — beeps when it needs him to take control, a bit like a dog wearing a smart collar.

And it’s confused. We are in the bowels of the Chrysler Technology Center in suburban Auburn Hills, Mich., navigating through the rabbit warren of a parking structure on the campus built by Lee Iacocca, the former Fortune posterboy who broke ground on the 500-acre site in 1986 and dedicated it in 1991, at a cost the company puts at about $1 billion. With the headquarters tower added in 1996, it spans 5.4 million square feet, the second-largest building in the U.S. by floor space, behind only the Pentagon.

Stellantis still runs its North American engineering out of Iacocca’s building, and the people who work there still say “all under one roof.” Inside, it’s a pure shot of early ‘90s design. Skinny escalators climb skyward around an octagonal skylight, like a Clinton-era MC Escher drawing.

The diamond-shaped parking garage attached to it is unique and confounding. Saha’s development mule heads toward the wrong exit and Saha has to put his hands on the wheel Even he finds the garage complicated. Auburn Hills’ suburban roads are much better for a test drive and I watch Saha’s mule smoothly navigate an intersection where two Michiganders decide to both make illegal multi-lane changes within seconds of each other.

Saha, the global engineering manager who serves as the owner of Stellantis’ L2++/hands-free door-to-door supervised automated driving system, has been at this longer than most. He worked on the Chrysler Pacifica that Stellantis supplied for Waymo’s first robotaxi in Arizona, then managed a group that integrated Level 4 autonomy with partners including Aurora and Lyft. He still test-drives every new software build himself, as often as twice a week, because he considers any problem a customer faces problems  to be his responsibility. He said his team built the Cherokee’s hands-free system in six weeks with the help of AI tools, when a similar project used to take a year or even 18 months.

He has a rule for AI, though: “I will not let people use AI to architect stuff because they will forget how to debug stuff,” he said. In a safety-critical business, he adds, engineers have to be able to answer every question.

Across two days of interviews at the technology center, engineers told Fortune that AI has turned yearlong projects into weeks and overnight simulations into minutes. Stellantis wants that speed to cut development time on its new computing and cockpit software, STLA Brain and STLA SmartCockpit as part of a general push to speed vehicle development from four years to 24 months, starting with two models in 2027. But nearly everyone who described a speed-up also described checking the machine’s work. Stellantis also has problems bigger than time savings. The company has 14 brands, a European business that is losing money, and a second-quarter adjusted operating margin of 1.8%, while CEO Antonio Filosa has set a margin target of 7% for 2030.

Wall Street isn’t waiting. Stellantis is the member of Detroit’s Big Three most exposed to Europe, which accounted for about 38% of its 2025 revenue. (GM sold its European brands, Opel and Vauxhall, in 2017 to PSA, one of the companies that later merged to form Stellantis.) Europe also leans much harder toward electric vehicles than truck-happy America: : battery-electric cars made up 17.4% of new EU registrations last year, according to ACEA, compared with 7.8% of U.S. sales, according to Cox Automotive.

Stellantis had also bet heavily on EVs in North America, and it took the biggest hit in Detroit after the $7,500 federal EV tax credit ended on Sept. 30, 2025. In February, Stellantis wrote down roughly €22.2 billion (about $26.5 billion), more than Ford’s $19.5 billion charge in December or the $7.6 billion GM took across two charges. Stellantis shares fell 25% that day, and the reverberations are still being felt, with the stock down nearly 60% year-to-date.

Mel Roberts, the director of North American infotainment and features planning, who plans the displays inside Stellantis vehicles five to eight years out, said AI was not her biggest surprise of the last several years. “What I couldn’t anticipate is just the complete collapse of the electrification ambitions and how that really did affect all of our future plans,” she said. “It trickled into everything.”

Stellantis is the only one of Detroit’s Big Three to be legally headquartered abroad, in the Netherlands. It’s the result of a pandemic-era merger in 2021 between Fiat Chrysler and the PSA Group that brought iconic European brands such as Peugeot and Citroën together with Fiat, Jeep and Ram. That gives it a distinctly international air, as Fortune met executives born in France, Mexico and Bangladesh within minutes of each other, along with a Michigander back from a few years stationed in Paris.

The mergers also left behind a machine built by committee. Ben Zawodni, manager of software engineering, is working to fold the hundreds of electronic control units, each a small computer with its own job, into a central “brain” called, naturally, STLA Brain. Over the decades, he says, the car’s architecture had evolved over time to really mirror the supply chain. “We were bolting on features.”

Amanda French, who leads the company’s platform teams, is tackling the same problem one layer down. Stellantis historically built separate platforms, each to a fixed size. Its new platform, STLA One, is built to stretch from small B-segment cars to midsize D-segment vehicles. The company says it is designed to grow into a mega platform supporting 30+ models and targeting more than 2 million units by 2035. Asked whether building it felt like playing with Legos, French responded, “Yeah, with a lot more people and emotions involved.”

Upstairs at the technical center, Chief Engineering & Technology Officer Ned Curic is a self-described “intense” but talkative and warm presence. He came to Stellantis by way of Amazon, with previous stints at Microsoft and Toyota. He explained that Stellantis is not where it needs to be. Some teams show “phenomenal successes,” he said. In building that culture, he said, “as a whole organization, we are not there.”

Curic sounds exasperated with an industry that has piled on complexity. Cars now come with “five screens, like digital noise, like 350 features,” he said, and automakers have historically tended to “checklist the heck out of the features” without measuring how people actually use them. He said he learned from Toyota that “the highest quality part that you have in a car is the part that you don’t have in a car.” In Stellantis’ research on drivers, for instance, he said most people preferred a mechanical stick to a button on a screen.

At Amazon, Curic received Jeff Bezos’ notorious emails forwarding on customer complaints. The body of each email was a single question mark. “I never found it stressful,” Curic said. “Never.” One executive would handle the problem, he explained, and the others would each write a couple of paragraphs to help.

From Amazon and Toyota, Curic also brought small teams from the “two-pizza rule” and single owners for each system, so engineers who once sat in separate groups can’t blame each other when something breaks. “If you see something that’s wrong, you just pick it up,” he said. “I own it.”

The hardest idea he’s selling is that “the best thing that you can do for your career is to make yourself redundant.” He has done it himself several times by getting a team in good shape, leaving, and starting something new. For that to work, Curic said, the company has to make sure there is always a new opportunity for those people, and that leaders need maturity and confidence. Asked whether Detroit’s long run of hard times makes people defensive about change, he replied that while there is always a bit of a fear, change is a lot more accepted, ”and actually sought after.”

The man telling engineers to make themselves redundant is also hiring them. At the Paris auto show in October, Curic told Bloomberg that Stellantis would add “multiple hundreds” of engineers in Europe and the U.S. this year.

The pressure lands on engineers like Zawodni and French. Both of them are tackling Stellantis’ tricky margins issue by simplifying the wiring for each vehicle to bring the manufacturing into alignment, cutting costs and boosting Stellantis’ profits back to where they need to be. “The AIs aren’t going to tell us what the new platforms are,” Zawodni said.

Zawodni said he started working on consolidating the cars’ central computing during COVID, when engineers went fully remote and Stellantis set up labs in India, Poland and North America that could be logged into from anywhere. A proof of concept for a global observability platform, which monitors software deep inside the car’s computers, took a week. Before agentic coding tools, he remembered something like that would take six months. And defects that took two to three weeks to fix shrank to two to three days. “We knew that we had to really reimagine all of our time,” Zawodni said. Did that scare him? “How exciting, right?”

French, a cheerful engineer from southern Indiana, lit up when the conversation turned to AI, though hers was a more measured take than Zawodni’s. She said human judgment “cannot be replaced,” but AI helps her pull together requirements and bills of materials stored in regional systems that were never built to talk to each other, because Stellantis is “made up from a number of different companies.” She compared AI to an interactive form of Cliffs Notes she wished for in school.

Zawodni said his team was not all as excited about the AI breakthroughs as he was. “I think there was a starting gun, and that starting gun went off,” he said. “Some people heard it, and some people didn’t.” Of his own engineers, he calls it a mixed bag. “Engineers are really afraid of losing their core skills,” he said. They want to know why a semicolon in a coding language does what it does. He called that “a valid curiosity,” but argued that it doesn’t get Stellantis to its goals. He wants them to become architects, and eventually chief architects.

The tools haven’t lightened Zawodni’s own load. “Agentic tools, they’ve made our work so much easier,” he said. “So why am I working so much harder?” He estimates he works at least twice as hard as before. “I feel a tremendous sense of urgency.” He said, “I really hope that we can transition responsibly … especially our people.”

Anne Laliron, a French engineer who runs Stellantis’ roughly 400-person tech research group, gave up her office after COVID so her team can always find her, and she lights up talking about their energy. Her job is deciding which big bets to make. Stellantis can’t afford to do everything, so it designs battery cells in-house and partners with startups for the rest. “If you want to embrace everything,” she said, “you are at risk of spreading your effort.”

For Stellantis, partnering is a way to punch above its weight. The company brings in Wayve, a British startup, for the perception software in its hands-free driving, works with the French startup Tiamat on sodium-ion batteries, with Zeta Energy on lithium-sulfur batteries, and owns a stake in the Chinese EV maker Leapmotor, selling its cars outside of China through the joint venture Leapmotor International. Laliron said the habit runs deep at Stellantis and is less common at other automakers. Curic wants a culture where “it doesn’t have to be invented here,” and he said the learning with Leapmotor runs both ways: “We learned a lot… we also taught them a lot.” Stellantis runs batteries the same way, Laliron said: design in-house, partner with startups, and leave mass production to its gigafactory partners.

Their biggest bet sits on a stage nearby: a battery-electric Dodge Charger prototype carrying a solid-state battery from Factorial, a Massachusetts startup Stellantis has worked with since 2021. The two companies run it as one team, and Factorial co-founder Siyu Huang says the startup has done it with $250 million in capital, a fraction of what some competitors have spent. The car worked the first time they turned the key. But Huang puts the technology three to five years from automotive production, and Laliron cuts about 10% of her group’s projects every year when they don’t pan out. “It’s always painful,” she said.

Elsewhere, the speed-ups are real, but still small next to Stellantis’ problems. Arturo Guzman was among the first to bring AI into the company’s aerodynamics work, about five years ago, after a startup struggled to explain it to him in a side conversation at a conference.

Now he explains it to vice presidents, and he starts by taking the mystery out. “There’s no miracles. There’s no magic,” he said. “For us being engineers, all this is a Python code.” Run through his team’s model, a design change to a Ram pickup’s front splitter returns a drag estimate in about three minutes. The full simulation used to take 14 to 24 hours. He tells his directors it’s like an intern. His younger engineers get a different metaphor: R2-D2 from Star Wars. “You just give it a task and come back and see what it did.”

Guzman said the time his team saves goes to “other stuff.” His team now generates new guidelines, takes requests from across the company, and mines its simulation data for patents. “Now I tell them, just send me the data,” he said.

Through the doors to the wind tunnel, the giant equipment runs at pretty much the same pace it always has. It still tests “typically, one car a day,” said Steve Kubiak, a deadpan Michigander who started at Chrysler in 1992 and has supervised the tunnel for about 10 years. Asked whether the process has changed over time, he said, “No, it’s always been the same.” The analysis is speeding up even if the testing isn’t. A colleague, Todd Lounsberry, gives AI the data from the last 20 runs of a test and asks what it sees. Asked how someone becomes the manager of a wind tunnel, Kubiak responded, “First you get a wind tunnel.”

Other engineers are keeping AI on a short leash. Mohammed Malik, who runs Stellantis’ driving simulators from the Automotive Research & Development Centre in Windsor, Ontario, said his group is “keeping it in the box,” but even so, technology has transformed his work. Malik at work is like a life-size, immersive game of Mario Kart, the classic racing game where Nintendo characters pick their car and track then try to dodge obstacles to the finish line.

His job has been transformed by his simulator more than by AI. Engineers used to tune a vehicle on a computer, build a prototype and only then find out how it felt. Now a driver can feel the computer model before anything is built, and Malik can swap springs on the fly. He can test 10 tires in an hour, something no prototype can do. His team has scanned about 20 roads, from racetracks to local streets, in 10-centimeter squares, and it trades models with colleagues in Brazil and Italy instead of shipping cars across oceans.

Malik plays me a video of a full-size Stellantis body that lacks any wheels — instead it’s suspended on what appear to be mechanical spider-legs, bobbing up and down, back and forth in front of a giant TV screen with a track. Asked whether he ever played Mario Kart, he said he has a track of his own, built by a student. “You can drive the Rainbow Road if you want,” he beams from behind his bushy mustache.

AI’s role is narrower. A simulator run produces thousands of channels of data, and when a car hits a bump and “swirls a little bit,” Malik asks AI which channel to look at. His ambition is much bigger: feed an agent every test driver’s scorecards from every region, ask it “what does it take to make a Jeep,” and let it drive the simulator itself until the answer feels right. For now, he said, the company is moving at a very slow pace and wants some form of control. “Some of the stuff we want to do, we can do today,” he said. “And some of the stuff we want to do, we cannot.”

The bigger surprise has been people’s willingness, or lack thereof, to adapt. Veteran test drivers who spent 10 or 20 years in physical prototypes were slow to move to the simulator. Young engineers with racing setups in their basements took to it right away. Laliron has seen the same thing. Experienced engineers carry old failures with them, she said, and sometimes “their brain is closing doors.”

Some people have made peace with work that is better but not faster. Roberts said her AI research tool returns 10 to 15 sources, and she has to check every one. “I don’t think it saves time,” she said, though it makes her work more “robust.”

Alison Rahm, the chief vehicle engineer for midsize and large SUVs, has seen this before. She is moving back to Michigan after two years running Stellantis’ European car lineup from Paris, and she remembers a staff meeting in 1997, when her boss told the room they were getting something new called email. “All of us were in a total panic,” she said. They went back to their desks and tried it anyway.

AI now runs checks that people used to do by hand, Rahm said, like going down a list of about 1,000 engineering design practices. That frees engineers to ask whether the rules themselves are right. But she isn’t ready to stop double-checking. For years after virtual crash testing arrived, she notes, engineers still crashed real cars into the walls to convince themselves the situations were right.

Asked how long it will take to trust AI the same way, Rahm paused. “I think we need another life cycle to prove to ourselves that our assumptions were right.” While cautioning that different products have different life cycles, she deliberated. “I would say four years.” That would land in 2030, the year Filosa has promised a 7% margin.

Saha drives us back into Iacocca’s garage, and puts his hands back on the wheel of the Cherokee as the diamond-shaped parking structure looms. The robot needs a guiding hand coming home.

Saha takes a long view on when the AI game will shake out. As we roll into a smooth parking job, he turns to me and says he’s a Game of Thrones fan (his favorite character is Robb Stark). While he works in logic, he explains, he likes fantasy because he finds he needs “to be a little bit philosophical” with the other side of his brain. “Creativity is very important.”

Saha takes a long view on when the AI game will shake out. As we roll into a smooth parking job, he turns to me and says he’s a Game of Thrones fan (his favorite character is Robb Stark). While he works in logic, he explains, he likes fantasy because he finds he needs “to be a little bit philosophical” with the other side of his brain. “Creativity is very important.”

Humans have adapted and thrived to date by figuring out creative solutions, he said. “We were never the strongest animal in the world,” he said, riffing a bit in the style of Game of Thrones writer George R.R. Martin. He suggests that several hundred years of industrialization led people sometimes to get used to process-oriented thinking. “My understanding is we’re going to leave behind the process-oriented world because AI is going to help us. And my personal belief is that’s actually good.”

“There will be some loss,” Saha said, as there is with any technological shift. But he pointed out that humans have adapted to the natural world through creativity over and over again. “People are going to figure out how to tame AI, too.”

[This report has been updated to clarify Ned Curic and Joydip Saha’s job titles with more specificity: Chief Engineering & Technology Officer and owner of L2++/hands-free door-to-door supervised automated driving, respectively.]

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5442. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5440. Data centers are learning to be flexible

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Data centers are driving up electricity demand, but flexible power use could ease grid congestion and speed up connections

Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Picture a soccer club that bought a passenger van for its tournaments a few times a year. The van sits in a driveway the rest of the year. Buying it was the right call, because a van that wasn’t there on tournament weekend would have stranded the team.

The American power grid works the same way, and now we have numbers to show just how little of it gets used. This month, under a new state law, Virginia’s utilities reported theirs. Over the year ending in July, the distribution grid run by Dominion $D Energy, the utility behind the northern Virginia data center boom, was being used at 41% of its capacity on average.

Even in its busiest hours, the system averaged 80%, with some pockets running higher and others lower. In the state’s rural southwest, where demand has been falling, Appalachian Power reported 14% for the year and 54% at peak.

Grids are sized for the few hours a year when everyone runs the air conditioner at once, and building for those few hours is expensive. A data center that pulls full power around the clock raises that peak, and raising the peak means buying another van that mostly sits in the driveway, costing money while it gathers dust.

Researchers argued there might be a cheaper route than building, and it required something we prize in people: Flexibility. Duke $DUK researchers calculated that the existing grid could absorb nearly 100 gigawatts of new demand if the newcomers agreed to cut back its power use for roughly half a percent of the year.

The study caused a stir in energy circles, and Google $GOOGL hired its lead author. The idea came down to a trade. A customer accepts being throttled in the few hours when the local grid is stretched, and in return connects in months instead of years.

The clearest track record of this working belongs to California’s PG&E. EV charging companies, which draw heavily on the grid, saw the wait for power fall to four to eight months from one to three years before its Flex Connect pilot.

In the pilot’s first two years, the power participants asked for was there nine hours out of ten. In the hours it wasn’t, the limits cut into operations less than 1% of the time.

Batteries offered another way to ease the pressure at peak. In 2025, a data center company in Oregon secured a faster hookup from Portland General Electric $GE by agreeing to add a 31-megawatt battery, enough to run about 25,000 homes for two hours, that it could switch to if needed.

Others flexed the computing itself. Google started by putting off work that could wait whenever grids in Belgium and Taiwan ran tight. In 2024, it dialed back machine learning jobs three times when the grid around Omaha was under strain. This year it promised five utilities it would hold back as much as a gigawatt of data center demand when the grid was stretched.

Startups are selling software that slow, pause or relocate AI jobs when the grid is tight. There were plenty of ways to do it, and more kept coming.

Flexibility is already becoming required in some regions. A 2025 Texas law requires new large data centers to install equipment that lets the grid operator cut their power remotely in emergencies. Late last year, FERC, the federal agency that regulates the grid, directed the operator PJM to create interruptible transmission options for data centers built next to power plants. The Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the Great Plains, made a similar move.

Of course, waiting is expensive, and data center queues in popular markets can run for years. Take an Nvidia $NVDA chip that costs $30,000 and is depreciated over three to five years, or $6,000 to $10,000 a year. Picture 100,000 of them in one cluster, waiting for power the way Microsoft $MSFT’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, said some of his company’s chips were last year. A year of waiting represents $600 million to $1 billion in potential computing value that goes unused.

The trade cost something on the other side too, although it was much less. For companies racing each other to build more powerful AI, even a few curtailed hours counted. If those 100,000 chips sat idle for the equivalent of 44 hours a year, the lost computing time would be worth $3 million to $5 million.

Flexibility will not fully replace the building the aging grid needs, because old equipment has to go regardless. But utilities planned to spend at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, with data centers and load growth among their top reasons, and a large transformer could take more than two years to arrive. Flexibility could shrink that bill, and that wait.

#5438. After the midterms, Big Tech’s AI data center problem is only getting bigger

After ChatGPT launched in late 2022, tech companies raced to open data centers at unprecedented rates, pouring billions of dollars into AI hubs in states like Texas and Ohio. Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and others did so even as polling showed the centers were highly unpopular among a large swath of the U.S. population.

On Tuesday, the issue came to a decisive tipping point. U.S. voters delivered an overwhelming victory for Democratic candidates throughout the country that will upend the halls of power in Washington and data center hotbeds like Texas. While tech companies have established years-long plans to keep opening the centers, and are regularly plugging more online, they will be met with new state and national political leaders whose mandate is to slow down the unpopular facilities. They also now face a wave of voter rejection on numerous projects across the U.S.

Voters sided against data center development in all but one of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts tracked by Redbud Consulting, a Washington, D.C., polling and data science firm, according to preliminary results.

That includes Piqua, a 20,000-person city in west central Ohio, where Meta is planning to spend $1 billion to construct a data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. Residents voted to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who supported the project.

In Ohio, voters in at least 14 municipalities approved data center bans or other restrictions, showing that the opposition extended well beyond a handful of high-profile projects.

And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott after campaigning on a moratorium on data center development until lawmakers establish additional protections for residents. Texas has more than 400 data center facilities and many more under construction, according to the American Edge Project and Technology Councils of North America.

“Most definitely, there will be challenges — two or three steps forward, one step back,” Baron Fung, senior research director at market research firm Dell’Oro Group, told Fortune, speaking about what Big Tech companies now face. “There could be delays … trying to address any kind of guidelines that weren’t really reinforced before regarding data centers.”

Fung said overall progress will continue, but companies may shift projects as they deal with pushback, and they will be asked to assume more of the financial and energy burden going forward rather than relying as much on municipalities.

Elon Musk, whose SpaceX expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditures in the quarter ending in December, wrote on X Tuesday night that “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Musk spent more than $200 million supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who lost.

The unpopularity of data centers in the U.S. has been a central theme of the AI revolution. Most Americans oppose data centers and are more fearful about AI than hopeful, according to recent Pew Research Center polls. During the second quarter of this year, at least 45 data center projects worth roughly $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs.

The hyperscalers opening the centers have themselves warned about disruptions to their plans. In September, Oracle executives noted during an earnings call that the company doesn’t assume every project will arrive on time, that it has backup options, and that it brings large campuses online in phases. The company has developments across the U.S. and internationally, so “all of our eggs are not in a single basket,” Co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said.

Oracle, in particular, has stood out for its risk-taking during the AI buildout, having more than $125 billion in debt and other notes payable and fundraising aggressively. Earlier this year, the company said it would need to raise between $45 billion and $50 billion in 2026 alone to fund its infrastructure expansion.

Before Tuesday’s election results, Microsoft, Amazon, and other major companies had mounted charm offensives in communities throughout the country in the hopes of winning over weary residents. The strategy has centered on money, utility-bill protections, local jobs, and transparency.

In October, Amazon announced “Built Together,” pledging more than $1 billion over five years to U.S. communities hosting its data centers. Amazon also pledged to publish its annual energy and water use, install lower-emission backup generators at new sites, and pay enough for power to avoid increasing other customers’ electricity bills.

In January, Microsoft promised to cover the power infrastructure costs associated with its facilities and stop seeking local property-tax breaks. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google also dropped requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements regarding data center projects.

That may not be enough in states like Texas. Incoming Gov. Hinojosa has called for repealing data center tax breaks and requiring developers to protect household utility bills and local water supplies, while giving residents more say over new projects.

“The impact may ultimately be less about restrictions than extracting more from data center operators for the social license to operate through taxes, power rates, environmental considerations, and community support,” analysts at investment banking firm Macquarie Group Limited wrote in a note Wednesday.

AI cloud providers could face higher rents for power-equipped data center buildings needed to fulfill customer contracts, potentially passing those costs on to customers, the analysts wrote. Demand from large cloud companies and AI labs could further tighten the supply of available sites. Big Tech companies may also fall back on upgrading or retrofitting existing data centers, Dell’Oro’s Fung said.

Many analysts and tech industry experts agree on one thing: Even with restrictions, AI centers are here to stay, especially as hyperscalers say they need more computing capacity online, not less. Amazon, Microsoft, Google parent Alphabet, and Meta are projected to spend between $720 billion and $740 billion in combined capital expenditures for calendar 2026.

In a call with analysts on Oct. 28, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said accelerating demand led the company to add 24 new data centers across five continents during the past quarter. A day later, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects revenue growth in the company’s cloud business to be 40% or more in 2027 and 2028, largely from AI.

“We’re installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up,” he said.

#5437. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5436. ‘Seismic’ blue wave triggers the sinking of oil prices, energy stocks, and the chances of power permitting reform

Most energy stocks plunged on Wednesday—except for clean power and utilities in a few remaining reliably red states—as crude oil prices fell to one-month lows because of bullishness on Iran war peace talks and bearishness on the data center boom after Democratic blue wave wins in the midterm elections.

Even as Wall Street celebrated the anticipated gridlock from a splintered Congress and White House—the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 3% Wednesday—most energy companies moved in the opposite direction, especially in states such as Texas that had the most shocking Democratic wins.

The other potential loser is the bipartisan legislation to expedite the construction of energy projects—and power the AI boom—that would benefit both renewable power and oil and gas pipelines. Anti-fossil fuel Democrats are now potentially motivated to take harder negotiating tactics. TD Cowen analysts slashed their projection for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) from 40% to 25% during the lame-duck session before the new Congress is sworn in.

Charles Hua, executive director of the PowerLines nonprofit, said the “seismic” blue wave from Congress to governors’ elections to public service commissions was a referendum on spiking utility bills, gasoline costs, and the inflationary ripple effects throughout the economy.

“You only get such seismicity in political results if something is fundamentally unsteady or unstable, and I think one of the big manifestations of that really has been energy costs,” Hua told Fortune.

In addition to voter discontent over the Iran war and fuel prices, there were more than 40 local ballot measure on restricting or regulating data centers. All but one of them—in North Dakota—passed. “That’s a staggering statistic,” Hua said.

As for Wall Street performance, there were clear winners and losers by utilities and independent power producers.

NRG Energy and Vistra, which are building out gas-fired power generation in Texas to help fuel the AI boom, saw their stock values drop precipitously by 12% and 15%, respectively. Gas turbine manufacturer GE Vernova dipped by 10%.

Analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies specifically highlighted the “Texas shock,” noting that “the most impactful surprise is the magnitude by which Texas voted Democratic, imperiling the outlook for data center developments.”

Texas-based Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk—after unsuccessfully spending hundreds of millions on GOP candidates—posted on X, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

On the other hand, utilities that operate in Florida, which remained Republican, were rewarded. Florida-based NextEra Energy jumped 5% and Duke Energy rose by 3%.

With more clean energy-loving Democrats coming into power, renewable energy companies also were rewarded. First Solar rose by over 4% and solar parts manufacturer Nextpower spiked by 13%.

After President Donald Trump downplayed the potential for an escalation in Iran and Vice President JD Vance blamed his party’s election losses on the war, the global oil benchmark fell by 8% to below $100 per barrel for the first time in nearly a month. As such, oil producers and refiners suffered on Wall Street too.

ExxonMobil and Chevron dipped by 4% and 5%, respectively. Refiners Marathon Petroleum and Valero Energy, which have reported record profits of late, plunged by 9% and 7%, respectively.

“We had a referendum on inflation, high oil prices, and Trump in general,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “It feels like Trump will have more pushback and less maneuverability around how he wants to conduct the conflict in Iran.”

There may be optimism for peace talks in Iran, but this war likely is far from over, Pickering warned.

There is no clear compromise yet, and Trump could easily get frustrated and opt for escalation between now and January, which is what Trump himself predicted before the election.

“I think the Iran conflict gets more complicated for the U.S. We’ve been looking for an off ramp, but we want an off ramp that doesn’t leave the Middle East in chaos,” Pickering told Fortune. “I think that issue probably transcends the election. Even with more Democrats, I don’t think they’re going to want a bad outcome for the Iran crisis. Oil is down, but it’s not cratering.”

Domestically, much of the focus will remain on the data center backlash and permitting reform. Some of the biggest states for data center growth are Texas, Georgia, and Ohio and Democratic challengers all won the governor elections in those states while pushing for data center moratoriums.

“‘Moratorium’ certainly is the buzzword,” Hua said, but it’s not clear if those efforts equate to temporary pauses or outright opposition. “How high on the priory list is electricity? I suspect that electricity vis-a-vis data centers will remain a top-of-mind issue for these new administrations.”

The AI boom has brought both parties somewhat closer together in terms of supporting all-of-the-above energy solutions. That’s why a bipartisan permitting reform effort focused on expediting energy construction of all kinds was coming together. But a Democratic wave is expected to leave more of them arguing in favor of waiting until next year to propose a version that’s less friendly to fossil fuel projects. Such an effort could be risky because it would still require Trump’s signature.

“With greater leverage heading into 2027, Democrats have less incentive to accept pipeline provisions during the lame duck, pushing the debate toward a narrower clean energy-transmission package or no deal,” Dumoulin-Smith added.

The legislation would facilitate the growth of long-distance transmission lines, which most benefit renewable energy. As such, top transmission developer Quanta Services saw its stock fall by 12% Wednesday.

The legislation’s Democratic sponsor, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., implored his party to still support the bill on Wednesday.

“Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises,” Whitehouse told Fortune in a statement. “It’s a bird in the hand. We’d be fools not to take it.”

Jordan Blum is the Energy editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of a growing global energy sector for oil and gas, transition businesses, renewables, and critical minerals.

#5434. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5433. How ‘Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch’ Turned a 60-Second Idea Into Broadcast TV Gold

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As ‘Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch” airs nationwide, its producer shares what he’s learned watching founders vie for life-changing investment.

This fall, our investment show, Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch, airs on more than 30 TV stations (ABC, CBS, FOX, CW) across the country — and it’s an accomplishment 10 years in the making. Started as a web series in 2016, this show is not only a testament to the startup mindset, but it is a sign that people love and are moved by stories of innovation, creativity, and tenacity. Over the past six seasons I’ve produced the show, I’ve been blown away by the energy and passion I’ve witnessed from both our contestants and our audience.

For those who don’t know the premise of the show, three angel investors sit on the top floor of a building where founders have just 60 seconds to pitch in an elevator on their way up. They have to state their mission, traction, revenues, and their ask before the clock runs out.

If they’re not able to win over the investors in those 60 seconds or if they totally freak out (which happens from time to time), the founder gets sent back down to the ground floor empty-handed.

But if the founder nails the pitch, the elevator doors open and they step into the boardroom to try to seal a deal. There are rapid-fire questions, financial rundowns and demos of products ranging from snacks to apps to hardware to category-defying ideas. If the entrepreneurs are able to dazzle the investors, negotiations and bidding wars begin, with offers ranging from $25,000 to $1 million flying around the room.

Over the past 10 years, Elevator Pitch has seen some of its winning companies soar, like Trexity (which grew from $1.6 million to $14 million), Amalfi Jets (which grew to 4 million overall social followers), and Autopilot (now valued over $1 billion).

I’ve been working in television for 15 years, and producing a show like this, getting it on broadcast TV, and helping founders realize their dreams has been one of the great privileges of my life. I hope that you will check your local listings and find our show. For entrepreneurs, it is a graduate class in pitching — find out what works and doesn’t work in the boardroom.

But don’t just take it from me — in the six weeks Elevator Pitch has been on the air, we have raced past the viewership ratings of lead-in programming in top markets like Los Angeles, New York, Chicago, Dallas and Philadelphia.

If you’re an entrepreneur, I hope watching will inspire you to put your pitch together and take a chance at completely changing the trajectory of your business. Apply to be on the new season here.

#5432. Appeals court tosses lawsuit over Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout, ruling homeowners can’t sue over notices

A New York appeals court on Wednesday threw out a lawsuit over the rollout of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax, ruling that the homeowners who sued had not adequately shown they were harmed.

The Appellate Division, Second Department, reversed a Sept. 29 judgment by Staten Island Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi that had granted the homeowners injunctive and declaratory relief. The four-judge panel was unanimous. It denied the petition and dismissed the case a week after hearing arguments.

Seven homeowners, represented by former First Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro, sued the city in August. They challenged the Department of Finance’s publication of a supplemental roll of about 900,000 properties and the roughly 17,000 notices it mailed to owners who might owe the surcharge, arguing the city made owners prove they live in their homes instead of checking its own records first.

The court did not rule on that argument. It found the homeowners lacked standing, or the legal right to sue, because they showed no concrete injury. Appearing on the roll or receiving a notice wasn’t enough, the judges wrote. The notice, court documents read, “serves an informational purpose,” like a debt collection letter, and the state legislature “must have anticipated that the list of notice recipients would not be exact or flawless,” or it would not have created an exemption process.

The court also said the rollout confusion was too “generalized, tenuous, and ephemeral” to count as an injury. It said the homeowners offered no evidence that anyone had misused the information or that they faced stalking or fraud, and it noted that the city’s annual assessment rolls already list each owner’s name, assessed value and market value. The court also said that the cost of applying for an exemption was not enough cause for injury, as all taxpayers spend time and money complying with tax rules, and the homeowners had not documented or quantified their costs.

Two of the seven petitioners, Rachel O’Brien and Carmine Morano, never alleged they received a notice. The other five were exempted after the suit was filed.

The panel sided with the homeowners on two points: It rejected the city’s argument that exempting the petitioners made the case moot, and its argument that the tax law limits challenges to appeals before the city’s Tax Commission. It also declined to decide whether DOF broke its own rule by not relying on 2024 income-tax data when it chose who got notices.

The ruling does not settle the tax’s other legal fights. Gothamist reported the surcharge faces three separate challenges.

The city has also changed course since the notices went out. After the state sent early 2025 income-tax data on Aug. 12, DOF cleared 1,210 owners and said it would send new letters to about 10,800 others. Gothamist reported that DOF has now granted more than 8,800 exemption requests. Comptroller Mark Levine estimated earlier this year the tax could raise up to $380 million from about 11,200 properties. Mamdani has said it will raise $500 million a year.

In a statement, Mamdani said the court “rejected an attempt by the ultrawealthy to avoid paying their fair share.” He added: “But owning a second home worth over $5 million should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable.”

He said the city will keep defending the law against “ongoing challenges in Suffolk County,” brought by “some of the same uberwealthy interests whose arguments just lost in court today.”

He closed: “We will implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone.”

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5431. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5430. Companies Are Paying Up to $1.45 Million for This In-Demand Job

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Demand for a specialized engineering role is driving impressive paychecks as companies compete for talent.

A highly sought-after engineering job is commanding a hefty price as employers compete to fill positions.

According to a recent Wall Street Journal report, demand for one specialized engineering role is pushing compensation into seven-figure territory. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) put agentic AI into production. They adapt AI tools to a company’s operations and help get those tools running.

Companies are increasingly bringing FDEs onto their own payrolls rather than relying on outside firms to make AI technology work, Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of recruiting firm Christian & Timbers, said in a new interview with the Journal.

Christian said top-notch FDEs are making between $586,000 and $1.45 million a year in total pay, with equity and bonuses comprising 52% to 66% of total pay.

Demand for FDE services has swelled as businesses discover they need hands-on support to put AI into practice. The engineers typically work for technology companies like Palantir or OpenAI, or consulting firms such as Accenture and McKinsey. However, Christian said other businesses are now hiring FDEs directly to develop AI applications internally.

The move to hire shifts the FDE job from a temporary one to a permanent responsibility. FDEs are now specialized in building reliable AI systems for a single employer and ensuring that the spending yields a financial return.

“Every company is thinking, ‘We got to do this ourselves,’” Christian said.

He added that hiring FDEs internally also allows businesses to keep their data private instead of sharing it with engineers supplied by outside vendors.

Recent job postings from Target, Barclays, Bausch and Lomb and American Express point to growing interest in hiring FDEs, per the Journal. The companies want engineers who can translate loosely defined objectives into working AI agent systems and expand experimental projects into tools used across their businesses.

Competition for these engineers is fierce, with corporate employers, technology companies and consulting firms all pursuing the same limited talent pool. Christian & Timbers estimates that the U.S. has about 17,000 FDEs, only around 2,000 of whom qualify as top-tier specialists.

At cloud-based data platform Snowflake, chief revenue officer Jonathan Beaulier told the Journal that recruiting FDEs was particularly difficult. The company’s frontier engineering group works directly with customers to develop AI applications. To help staff that team, the company is drawing on employees from other divisions, he said.

Growing demand for FDEs has helped create businesses such as Distyl AI, founded by former Palantir employees Arjun Prakash and Derek Ho. The startup places engineers inside client companies to help shape their AI plans and build the tools to carry them out.

“The most common question being asked by the CEO of a Fortune 500 today is not, ‘How do I deploy AI?’ It’s actually, ‘What should my business model be?’” Prakash said in an interview with the Journal. “That partnership requires a certain flavor of forward-deployed engineering with a heavier strategy muscle.”
