#5429. I believe in AI. But my AI assistant gave me more work than it could finish

Dr. Morissa Schwartz is an entrepreneur, author and AI strategist who founded GenZ Publishing and the communications firm Dr. Rissy’s Writing & Marketing. She holds a doctorate in literature and was named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list in Media in 2022.

I opened my daily to-do list and found 156 items.

“Daily” was doing some ambitious work in that sentence.

I’m a writer, publisher and entrepreneur. I expect a certain amount of chaos. There are manuscripts, emails, projects, follow-ups and the occasional administrative mystery that arrives disguised as a perfectly ordinary Tuesday.

Still, 156 items suggested that my productivity system had developed career ambitions of its own. It was building a department. Soon it would need an org chart.

Some of the work was already underway. Some items overlapped. Some were reminders about other reminders. Tasks that belonged together had become separate obligations, each carrying the emotional weight of an unfinished thing.

I had asked for help getting work done. I was getting very good at maintaining evidence that work existed.

I use AI, and I remain a big believer in what it can do. It helps organize ideas and get thoughts onto a page. Technology that makes expression and work more accessible matters to me.

That is why I want to be honest about the less glamorous part: an assistant can generate work faster than it can finish it.

Ask it to help with a project, and it may produce a plan. Ask it to improve the plan, and it may produce a checklist. Ask it to make sure nothing gets missed, and the checklist may develop subcommittees.

Every item can sound reasonable on its own. Collectively, they can turn help into a second job.

The problem starts with an easy confusion: identifying the next step feels like progress.

Sometimes it is. A clear plan can get a stuck project moving. But a plan also has a comforting property: it can be created without confronting the hardest part of the work.

A draft can sit there looking polished. A calendar can fill up with preparation. A task can be checked off because someone wrote instructions for completing it.

Meanwhile, the email still needs sending. The application still needs submitting. The client still needs the finished file.

A productivity system earns its keep when those things happen.

After the 156-item surprise, I started insisting on a more useful question: What would “done” look like to the person who asked for this?

For an article, that could mean a finished draft, if a draft was requested. If the request was to pitch it, “done” includes an actual pitch. If the request was to publish it, a document called FINAL_FINAL_REALLY_FINAL does not quite complete the journey.

The distinction sounds obvious. It gets surprisingly slippery once work passes through several tools, checklists and assistants.

First, I want a daily list that reflects available capacity.

For assistant execution, I’m aiming for roughly 25 meaningful entries on a weekday, while preserving real deadlines and necessary daily operations. The number is a working limit for my system, rather than a productivity prescription for everyone.

Its purpose is to force a choice. If everything is due today, the list has stopped helping me decide what to do today.

Flexible work can live in a backlog with a reasonable checkpoint. Waiting for someone’s response deserves a waiting status. A genuine deadline deserves space that has not already been occupied by 40 vaguely urgent reminders.

A campaign may involve research, outreach, tracking and follow-ups. Those requirements still matter. Putting them under one clear execution item can preserve the work while reducing the number of separate things shouting at me.

The details should remain available when they are useful. I don’t need every detail to greet me at the top of the stairs.

Third, I want proof attached to completion.

If an assistant says an email was sent, I should be able to see it. If it says something was published, I need the live link. If it says a file was delivered, I need the usable file and the delivery record.

That proof also helps prevent duplicate work. A system that remembers what actually happened can stop proposing the same action with slightly different punctuation.

“Unable to complete” gives me another mystery to manage. “The form requires an answer only you can provide” gives me a decision. “This browser session cannot access the account” identifies an access problem.

The next question is whether anything else can move forward. One missing answer should not freeze every unrelated part of a project.

Finally, I want the system to count outcomes.

How many pitches actually went out? Which replies need an answer? What has been accepted? Which deliverables reached the client? What remains unfinished?

I care about those numbers because they describe the work I was trying to accomplish. A magnificent list of possible actions describes the system’s imagination.

These changes require judgment. Some days have more real deadlines. Some tasks take minutes; others need uninterrupted hours. A short list can still be unrealistic, and a long checklist can be useful inside a complicated project.

The goal is a system that helps me see the difference.

AI can be extraordinarily helpful here. It can reconcile records, find overlaps, preserve context and handle routine steps. But it needs instructions that reward finishing, checking and communicating honestly about what remains.

It also needs permission to stop manufacturing another plan when the next useful action is already clear.

I still want an assistant. I still want technology to make work easier and possibilities bigger.

I would just like my to-do list to stop recruiting.

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

Getting people past the velvet rope is the family business. Stacy’s father, Bill Fischer, founded the company as Fischer Travel more than 60 years ago. But white-glove service doesn’t come cheap. “We’re not a discount shop,” Max says. “But if you want access, if you want to be able to walk into a hotel and not check into a front desk and just go straight to the room, that’s the service that we provide.”

#5426. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5425. LIVE – Bitcoin Price Slides, Washington’s Political Balance Shifts, Trump’s Crypto Agenda at Risk

Bitcoin price fell toward $75,700 as Democrats captured the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, raising fresh uncertainty over Trump’s crypto agenda. But Bitcoin has now recovered to $77,700 during Asian trading hours, but remained under pressure as Nasdaq futures plunged and investors reassessed Washington’s political balance.

Democrats secured control of the Senate in a sweeping rebuke to President Donald Trump, winning key races in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Kansas and South Carolina. The House outcome remained closely contested, with Democrats also making significant gains.

The result threatens to complicate Trump’s push for clearer crypto regulations. Bitcoin price weakness now reflects both market risk aversion and concerns that Congress could delay legislation designed to establish a federal framework for digital assets.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin briefly dropped more than $2,000 after early election results pointed toward a Democratic victory, falling from nearly $78,000 to the $75,000 level. Buyers subsequently stepped in, lifting BTC toward $77,700 this morning.

The selloff extended beyond crypto markets. Nasdaq 100 futures dropped as much as 2.3%, while S&P 500 futures fell 1.3% as investors reacted to the possibility of tighter oversight of technology companies and AI infrastructure projects.

BREAKING: The S&P 500 is now on track to open below 7,500 for the first time since July 31st as markets price-in a Democrat victory in both the House and Senate.Nasdaq 100 futures are now down more than -2% tonight. pic.twitter.com/mBbq77a2mG

The dollar also weakened, while the 10-year Treasury yield slipped six basis points to around 4.90%. The moves raised concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress could limit Trump’s tax and spending agenda, while increasing regulatory scrutiny across several industries.

Bitcoin’s decline followed an already difficult period for digital assets. The king had slipped below $77,000 earlier in the week as technology stocks weakened and investors reduced exposure to riskier assets.

The election adds another source of uncertainty, although Bitcoin’s recovery from its overnight low shows people have not fully abandoned the market.

The biggest crypto-specific concern involves the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act, which aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and divide oversight responsibilities between U.S. regulators.

The legislation failed to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September, falling short of the 60 votes required. Democrats opposed the measure over concerns about ethics provisions and Trump’s crypto-related business interests.

A Democratic-controlled Senate could make the bill’s path more difficult, particularly if lawmakers prioritize stronger safeguards and additional oversight of the crypto industry.

The election also gives Democrats greater power to investigate the administration and examine potential conflicts of interest involving Trump’s digital asset ventures. Congressional scrutiny could intensify even without new legislation.

However, the result does not automatically mean crypto regulation will become more restrictive. Democrats have supported regulatory frameworks for digital assets, but disagree with Republicans over enforcement, consumer protections and safeguards against political conflicts.

The immediate risk is that negotiations become slower and more complicated, leaving crypto firms without the regulatory clarity they have sought.

Bitcoin price direction will likely depend on whether the election-driven selloff spreads into a deeper market correction. A sustained recovery in Nasdaq could help Bitcoin regain momentum, particularly if investors begin treating the election result as a temporary source of uncertainty rather than a lasting threat to risk assets.

On the other hand, continued weakness in technology stocks could pressure BTC and altcoins further. Investors will also watch whether Democrats pursue aggressive investigations or push for substantial changes to crypto legislation.

The political shift could create a more difficult environment for Trump’s crypto agenda during the final two years of his presidency. Yet a divided government may also limit sweeping policy changes from either party.

For now, Bitcoin price remains caught between broader market weakness and uncertainty over U.S. crypto regulation. The election has changed the political landscape, but the next moves in Congress will determine whether the impact becomes a lasting obstacle for the industry.

#5424. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5423. How Abdul El-Sayed would build Medicare for All, from a wealth tax to a Fed-style governing board

Near the end of his victory speech in Detroit early Wednesday, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed returned to the line that carried his campaign: “It shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world.”

El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s open Senate race on a night when Democrats captured both chambers of Congress. He arrives in Washington as one of the country’s most prominent advocates of Medicare for All, a public, universal, single-payer system, and as the co-author of a detailed plan for how it would work.

The issue resonated with voters in both parties. In the NBC News Exit Poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters, 85% said they were very or somewhat concerned about healthcare costs. Sixty-one percent said the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get it.

Democrats campaigned on healthcare costs across the country, but the party is split on the fix. Many moderates want to strengthen the Affordable Care Act, which expanded coverage through Medicaid and subsidized private marketplaces. For El-Sayed and other progressives, Medicare for All remains the gold standard, and a single public payer would replace much of the private insurance business that sustains some of America’s largest companies.

UnitedHealth Group is No. 3 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the biggest healthcare company on the list. CVS Health, which owns Aetna, ranks No. 6, and Elevance Health ranks No. 18. El-Sayed has singled out the industry before: in 2022, in written testimony to the Senate Budget Committee, he noted that UnitedHealth’s second-quarter profit in 2020 nearly doubled from a year earlier.

El-Sayed, 42, holds a medical degree and a doctorate, ran Detroit’s health department from 2015 to 2017, and later directed Wayne County’s Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services. He and co-author Micah Johnson laid out their vision in the 2021 book Medicare for All: A Citizen’s Guide, which offers the clearest picture of how the policy could take shape as progressives grow in Congress.

In the book, El-Sayed and Johnson describe Medicare for All as “an enhanced version of the traditional Medicare program that tens of millions of seniors rely on today,” one that would insure every American for life.

A “core tenet” of the policy, they write, is comprehensive coverage: physician visits, prescription drugs, and emergency services, potentially extending to long-term care, vision, and dental. Patients could see any participating provider, eliminating out-of-network charges.

El-Sayed has also pitched the system as more durable than employer-based coverage. “Turn 26, get a job, lose a job, get married, get divorced: none of these would cost you your health insurance under Medicare for All,” he wrote in the same Senate testimony.

One element has shifted. In a 2020 podcast, El-Sayed said Medicare for All “does away with the private insurance market,” Bridge Michigan reported. During this campaign, he said his version would not ban private plans offered through unions or employers, though his campaign website says Medicare for All “should make those choices redundant and unnecessary.”

He has also sketched how the system would be run. At a July roundtable with Michigan voters hosted by More Perfect Union, El-Sayed said its governance should sit “under, but separate from, the executive branch,” similar to the Federal Reserve, so the program couldn’t “change on a dime” with each new president. He added that Medicare would negotiate prescription drug prices as the buyer for the entire country.

El-Sayed and Johnson argue that individual Americans already fund the U.S. healthcare system through taxes, premiums, deductibles, and copayments. Under Medicare for All, they contend, money would flow through the public sector rather than private insurers.

Their financing plan has two parts. The first would “combine existing federal spending on Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance subsidies into a single stream to be used for Medicare for All.” The authors also float administering the program at the state level, which would free up state money now spent on Medicaid and private insurance.

The second is progressive taxation: a “wealth tax on the richest Americans,” a new corporate tax code, and higher taxes on investment income. The authors also count on savings from lower administrative costs and lower prices for drugs and services, which they attribute to a single payer’s negotiating power.

The middle-class question is unresolved. El-Sayed has said he would “hope” to avoid raising taxes on most Michigan families, including those earning around $100,000 a year, according to Bridge Michigan. Experts told the outlet that middle-class tax increases would likely be necessary, though some households could come out ahead overall.

El-Sayed has been blunt about the obstacle. “The biggest challenge is not making the math work. The biggest challenge is not architecting the system. The biggest challenge is creating the political will to get there,” he told the More Perfect Union panel, which included several voters who had backed President Trump.

Public opinion is moving in his direction. In an Axios-Ipsos poll released in October, 43% of Americans supported Medicare for All and 24% opposed it, with 32% unsure.

The policy still has vocal critics, from pharmaceutical companies to the American Hospital Association. They argue that dismantling private insurance would eliminate jobs in healthcare administration and that middle-class families would bear the brunt of higher taxes. They also point to the price tag. A 2018 analysis by Charles Blahous, a former public trustee for Medicare and Social Security, estimated that Bernie Sanders’ Medicare for All proposal would add $32.6 trillion in federal spending over 10 years. Blahous has described that figure as a lower bound that assumes the bill’s cost controls deliver their full savings.

The votes are another hurdle. Democrats will control both chambers in January, but Republicans and many moderate Democrats oppose single-payer. Retiring Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell called it an “untested government takeover” in 2019. Any bill would likely need 60 votes to clear a Senate filibuster, plus President Trump’s signature.

Still, El-Sayed won’t be alone. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson unseated Republican Sen. Susan Collins after campaigning on Medicare for All and told the American Prospect he would be a “dog with a bone” on the issue. The next test is whether the new progressive senators rally behind a single bill, and whether El-Sayed’s room for private plans becomes a compromise or a fault line.

“Winning a single U.S. Senate seat was never the goal,” El-Sayed told supporters early Wednesday. “The goal is to use that seat to transform our politics.”

#5422. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5421. Replacing Entry-Level Talent With AI Is a Costly Mistake. Here’s What to Do Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is changing how businesses think about hiring, but eliminating junior roles can create problems that outweigh the short-term savings.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you ask a group of business leaders where AI should fit within their teams, many will give the same reply: It can take over the kind of work we used to assign to interns. This view is easy to understand. AI is good at research, summaries and first drafts, so the entry-level role starts to look optional. However, I believe that’s a mistake — and an expensive one.

Cutting junior roles may save money this year. It also removes two things AI can’t replace: those people who see your business with fresh eyes, and the pipeline that produces your future managers.

The most obvious objection is that an AI tool costs less than a salary and doesn’t require onboarding. And yes, if you only look at this year’s budget, replacing junior roles can look like a smart call.

The problem is what that decision costs later. Every senior person on your team started their career somewhere. As Lucy Beaumont, global SVP of product at SHL, told CNBC, entry-level roles are where people make their first mistakes and learn how a business really runs.

If nobody is trained today, who will be leading in 10 years? Cut that training ground, and you’re left with two options: Pay a premium to poach experienced people from competitors, or promote people who never learned the basics.

Meanwhile, graduates get stuck in a loop: Roles ask for experience, and experience requires someone to take a chance and hire them. ZipRecruiter’s 2026 graduate report found that 81.6% of grads who worked during college are now employed, compared with 40.7% of those who didn’t. So someone has to break the loop, and the companies that do get first pick of loyal, motivated talent other employers overlook.

Experienced teams run on routine, and that’s a big part of what makes them efficient. The trade-off is that familiar processes rarely get a second look, even when there’s a better way to do them.

New employees have the benefit of fresh eyes and a fresh perspective. They notice onboarding steps with unnecessary friction or features customers will never use. They then ask, “Why do we do it that way?” and sometimes this leads to new and improved processes.

Of course, I have a bias; I joined AnswerConnect in 2006 as a temp-to-hire with little experience. Early on, the founder asked how things were going and really listened when I shared feedback on pain points I had experienced. I saw almost immediate changes, and the idea that I could make a difference as a brand-new employee changed everything for me. I chose to stay, and I’ve grown throughout the organization and helped influence change along the way. This is baked into our company culture and makes us stronger.

None of this means avoiding AI. It means using it to improve junior roles, not eliminate them.

Leave the role in place and redesign it instead. Make a list of the actual activities entry-level employees carry out each week. Pass repetitive tasks to AI, and return the time gained to the kinds of work where people develop fastest, such as talking to customers, solving problems and making judgment calls.

Teach new employees to use AI critically. Teach them to check AI output, recognize when it is incorrect and know when a person should stay involved. These skills will only become more valuable, and they’re easier to develop early on than to correct later.

Don’t leave new hires to work it out alone. Build learning into the job from day one: working sessions with experienced colleagues, shared projects and paid time for training. Your senior people benefit, too. You often realize how you do something could be better when you explain it.

Encourage curiosity and feedback. Make it easy for new hires to tell you what they see:

Every business will use AI. What matters is what you do with the time and money it frees up: bank the savings and shrink the team, or invest in the people who’ll be running your company in 10 years.

People who are trained and trusted care more, and customers can tell. So which company will you be: the one that stopped developing talent, or the one that built it?

#5420. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5419. Your First Instinct in a Crisis Is Probably Wrong. Here’s What Strong Leaders Do.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

What do you do when your first reaction goes sideways?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

You probably believe you will be the calm one when something goes wrong. You picture yourself absorbing the bad news, asking the right questions and setting a steady course while everyone around you scrambles. Then the phone rings late on a Friday, and the first thing that happens is not a thought. It is a reaction.

That reaction feels like clarity. It shows up instantly, it carries total confidence and it arrives with a jolt of urgency that makes waiting feel irresponsible. The trouble is, it often solves a different problem than the one in front of you. Learning to notice that gap, and to cross it on purpose, is one of the most useful skills you can build as a leader.

Under acute stress, your body does what it was built to do. Your heart rate climbs, your attention narrows and your brain favors speed over nuance. That response works well when a threat is physical and immediate. It works poorly when the threat is ambiguous, involves many people and will unfold over days or weeks.

Narrow focus helps when danger is right in front of you. It becomes a liability when the information you need is scattered across a team, a customer inbox and a conversation that has not happened yet. In that moment, the urge to act right now can feel like leadership. More often, it is discomfort looking for an exit. Panic rarely leads to sound choices, which is why staying calm lets you lead a team through a crisis rather than react.

Most crisis missteps fall into a few familiar patterns.

The first is the urge to fix it immediately. Speed feels responsible, but acting before you understand the scope often creates a second problem on top of the first.

The second is the urge to explain everything. When you feel exposed, you want to fill the silence with context and justification. Long explanations offered early tend to sound defensive, and they lock you into details that may change as more facts surface.

The third is the urge to find out who is at fault. Assigning blame can feel like taking control, yet it shifts your team’s energy from solving the problem to protecting themselves.

The fourth is the urge to go quiet. Silence can feel safe, but the people who depend on you will fill an information vacuum with their own assumptions and those assumptions are rarely generous.

The goal is not to ignore your first instinct. It is to give it a brief review before it becomes a decision. In most situations, even serious ones, you have more time than the adrenaline suggests. Ninety seconds is almost always available.

Use that window to ask three questions. What do I actually know, versus what I fear? Who is affected, including people who have not said anything yet? What happens if I wait one hour before responding publicly?

It also helps to look at the problem the way an outsider would. Stepping outside your role for a moment creates enough distance to separate facts from feelings. Write down what you know on one side of a page and what you assume on the other. The second column is usually longer than you expect.

None of this means waiting for perfect information. You will rarely have it, and acting decisively, then adjusting as you learn, usually beats freezing. The point is to make your first move considered rather than reflexive.

The second instinct, the one that arrives after the initial surge passes, is usually better calibrated. It considers the timeline. It accounts for the audience. It notices what you can control and what you cannot.

You can strengthen that second instinct long before any crisis arrives. Decide in advance who has the authority to speak, who needs to be in the first conversation and where the reliable facts will live. Talk through a few plausible scenarios with your team while everyone is calm. When the real moment comes, you’ll choose from options you have already considered instead of inventing them under pressure.

It also helps to spread the thinking around. Leaders who listen actively and push decisions closer to the people with firsthand information tend to see problems more completely. The person closest to the issue often knows something you don’t, and a crisis is the worst time to discover you never asked.

Teams that handle difficult moments well rarely have to improvise. They simply have to improvise less.

When things settle, people rarely recall the exact words you used. They remember whether your response felt proportionate, whether you addressed their real concern and whether your account held up as new information emerged. Employees, customers and partners who never said a word watch for the same thing: evidence that you handled the situation with care and judgment.

That impression forms quickly, often within the first day, and it is built from small choices. Your first instinct will rarely get it all right. A short, deliberate pause gives you a much better chance.

You probably believe you will be the calm one when something goes wrong. You picture yourself absorbing the bad news, asking the right questions and setting a steady course while everyone around you scrambles. Then the phone rings late on a Friday, and the first thing that happens is not a thought. It is a reaction.

That reaction feels like clarity. It shows up instantly, it carries total confidence and it arrives with a jolt of urgency that makes waiting feel irresponsible. The trouble is, it often solves a different problem than the one in front of you. Learning to notice that gap, and to cross it on purpose, is one of the most useful skills you can build as a leader.

Under acute stress, your body does what it was built to do. Your heart rate climbs, your attention narrows and your brain favors speed over nuance. That response works well when a threat is physical and immediate. It works poorly when the threat is ambiguous, involves many people and will unfold over days or weeks.

#5418. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

#5417. The Hidden Risks of Building Your Own Delivery Fleet as a Growing Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Building an in-house delivery fleet may seem like a smart way to reduce costs and gain greater control, but these challenges can quickly impact profitability.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The invoices from the regional carrier keep getting bigger. For the owner of a growing home furnishings retailer, delivery has become one of the largest expenses outside of inventory, and the complaints that come with it — missed windows, damaged pieces, vague updates — still land on her desk.

So she runs the numbers on three cargo vans and three full-time drivers. On paper, the savings look obvious. What the spreadsheet leaves out is that she is not just buying vans. She is starting a transportation operation inside a company built to sell furniture.

The case for in-house delivery is legitimate. You decide when orders go out and how customers are treated at the door. You depend less on a third party’s capacity during busy weeks, you can coordinate dispatch directly with inventory, and at sufficient volume, you may lower your cost per delivery.

The catch is that an outside carrier bundles its costs into a price per stop. Once you own the operation, those costs scatter. Maintenance appears in repair invoices, insurance in renewal paperwork, depreciation on the balance sheet and recruiting and supervision both in payroll and in the owner’s calendar. Vehicles also sit idle on slow days and break down on busy ones.

In-house delivery is not automatically cheaper. Build a fully loaded cost per delivery that includes idle time, downtime, fuel, insurance, depreciation and management hours, then compare it with outsourced pricing across slow weeks as well as peak ones. A model built on your best month will flatter the fleet.

The same principle applies to broader ecommerce operations. Growing order volumes require companies to reconsider operational processes, technology investments and cost structures.

With two vans, the owner knows who drove which route and when the oil was last changed. That informality works, which is why it tends to persist long after it should be replaced.

At 10, 20 or 50 vehicles, decisions that once lived in one person’s head need to live in a system. Assign ownership for scheduling, maintenance, driver qualification files and performance. In a smaller operation, that may be one capable operations manager, but it must be a named role. Then track a short list of numbers: on-time rate, cost per delivery, vehicle downtime and incidents. Without them, you are managing by anecdote.

This transition reflects a broader challenge of business expansion. Building systems and teams that scale successfully emphasizes the importance of repeatable processes, clear responsibilities and infrastructure that can support increasing operational demands.

A driver is often the only person from your company a customer meets, and also the person operating a heavy vehicle on public roads with your inventory inside. Informal hiring does not scale. A repeatable process does.

Define written qualification criteria, including license status, driving history review where permitted and experience suited to your vehicles, and apply them to every candidate. Onboarding should cover cargo height and clearance, securing loads, customer handoffs and what to do when something goes wrong.

Put your standards for company vehicle use in writing, including phone use, personal use and defect reporting. Some vehicle sizes and operations trigger additional federal or local requirements, so verify what applies to your fleet.

Imagine a company that advertises tight two-hour windows and stacks routes to hit them. It works until a customer isn’t home or a freeway slows. Now the driver is behind, and the easiest way to recover is to speed up, skip a break or glance at a phone.

Fleet safety is partly a scheduling problem. If your routes only work when nothing goes wrong, you have designed in pressure. A few practical fixes help:

Tight windows can remain a selling point where routes are dense and predictable.

Reliable delivery also depends on operational consistency. Efficient workflows and well-organized teams help businesses maintain service standards as demand increases.

Relying on drivers to notice mechanical problems works for a few vehicles. It fails once drivers rotate through different vans and each assumes someone else reported the strange noise.

Set preventive service intervals based on manufacturer guidance and actual use. Require a short pre-trip inspection and make defect reporting penalty-free. Keep records in one place so patterns become visible, such as a van that keeps returning to the shop. Decide in advance that a vehicle with a safety-related problem comes out of service, even on a heavy day.

Then plan for downtime. A spare vehicle, a rental arrangement or an outside carrier on standby keeps one broken van from becoming a week of broken promises. Customers experience your maintenance program as reliability.

Most owners picture an accident as a repair bill. The real cost is wider: employee injuries, injuries to other road users, vehicle replacement, insurance claims and possible premium changes, delayed orders, lost productivity, administrative work and reputational damage. Depending on the circumstances, it can also raise legal questions, which is one reason consistent records matter.

The human side deserves honest attention. Delivery vans and box trucks are often heavier and taller than the passenger cars around them, and the injuries associated with commercial vehicle collisions, including head trauma, spinal damage and fractures, can change someone’s life and disrupt a business for a long time.

A one-page accident procedure, reviewed with every driver, should answer a few questions:

A business that outsources delivery pushes much of its transportation risk onto the carrier. Once you operate your own vehicles, that risk is yours to evaluate.

Work with a qualified broker to review limits, exclusions, covered drivers and how cargo is treated. Pay particular attention to the difference between company-owned vehicles and employees’ personal vehicles used for business, since those situations are often treated differently. Requirements and policy terms vary by jurisdiction and insurer, so confirm the details for your own operation.

Insurance also cannot replace good systems. Coverage helps absorb a loss. It does nothing to prevent the missed inspection, the rushed route or the untrained hire.

Sustainable growth requires systems that can operate consistently without constant intervention from the business owner. This principle is explored in an Entrepreneur article about building repeatable systems for long-term business growth, highlighting the importance of documenting, evaluating and continuously improving business processes.

Owning vehicles buys control, but control only pays off through discipline: clear ownership, consistent hiring, realistic schedules, preventive maintenance, an accident plan and a sober view of cost. The businesses that succeed with in-house delivery do so because they built a system around their vans, not because they bought good ones.

The invoices from the regional carrier keep getting bigger. For the owner of a growing home furnishings retailer, delivery has become one of the largest expenses outside of inventory, and the complaints that come with it — missed windows, damaged pieces, vague updates — still land on her desk.

So she runs the numbers on three cargo vans and three full-time drivers. On paper, the savings look obvious. What the spreadsheet leaves out is that she is not just buying vans. She is starting a transportation operation inside a company built to sell furniture.

The case for in-house delivery is legitimate. You decide when orders go out and how customers are treated at the door. You depend less on a third party’s capacity during busy weeks, you can coordinate dispatch directly with inventory, and at sufficient volume, you may lower your cost per delivery.

#5415. Airbnb’s Brian Chesky Says He Was ‘Naturally a Terrible CEO.’ Here’s What Makes the Job So Hard — And What’s a ‘Death Sentence.’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The Airbnb chief executive opened up about his shortcomings as a leader.

Brian Chesky has been the CEO of Airbnb since the company’s inception in 2007. For nearly 20 years, he has stuck with the top job and overseen Airbnb’s incredible growth to become a company with over 5.5 million hosts and $12.24 billion in annual revenue in 2025.

However, being a CEO didn’t come naturally. In a recent interview with the How I Built This podcast, Chesky opened up about his shortcomings as a leader when Airbnb first got started.

Chesky drew a distinction between being a great founder and being a great CEO.

“I think I was pretty much naturally a great founder and I was naturally a terrible CEO,” he said on the podcast.

Chesky pointed out that someone could spend their “whole life” being a founder. It starts in childhood, with making and building things — all prep work for being a founder. The moment a person creates a company is probably not the first time they try to make something, Chesky said. He estimated that when he started Airbnb at age 26, he probably had “20 years of experience as a founder, starting as a child designing, disassembling Christmas toys.”

By the time he founded the company, he claimed to have had decades of experience with founding or creating something under his belt.

Then came the tougher challenge: being CEO. Chesky said on the podcast that the main problem with being a CEO is that it is so counterintuitive.

“For example, people tell you to hire great people and trust them and get out of their way to do their job,” Chesky said. “That is what you do once you are very mature. That is a death sentence to a young company.”

Chesky said that good CEOs actually have to be strategic in making new hires. They have to steer away from hiring experienced people who don’t understand the company. Instead, they have to hire workers a “little bit ahead” of them who are smart and hungry — and then “stay really close to them.”

Chesky also addressed the question of how CEOs can create a culture where employees automatically do what is expected of them, even when the CEO isn’t in the room.

“That’s the hard stuff,” he said. “That’s really hard. Not becoming profitable, expense management — that stuff is easy.”

Chesky admitted that early on, he was “cautious” about being a boss. He “felt shy” about directing people to do something, especially workers who seemed older and more experienced.

“I think I was a little bit of a people pleaser,” he said. “I wanted people to like me.”

The difficult part for Chesky was when his intuition would clash with what his employees were telling him. Usually he deferred to their experience, and usually it was a mistake, he said.

“My intuition is telling me this thing,” Chesky said. “It doesn’t mean you’re wrong, but now let’s talk about it.

#5413. The AI Race Is No Longer About Better Models. Here’s Where the Real Value Is Being Created.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As AI models mature, the true battleground has shifted from raw intelligence to real-world deployment.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the past three years, the AI story was a race to build a better model. Every few months, a company released one that was faster, smarter and cheaper. In 2026, the story changed. The biggest AI announcements of the year were not new models at all. They were new companies built for one purpose — putting engineers inside other companies to make AI work there.

In May 2026, OpenAI launched a new company for this, backed by more than $4 billion. Its engineers move into a customer’s business, learn how the work really gets done and stay until the AI works in day-to-day use. Days earlier, Anthropic announced a similar company of its own, built for mid-sized businesses that do not have enough technical staff to do this work themselves.

These engineers have a name: forward-deployed engineers. The idea started at Palantir. Instead of selling software and wishing the customer luck, the engineer sits with the customer’s own team and connects the AI to the company’s real information and real way of working. They are not judged on advice or presentations. They are judged on one thing — whether the system still works when real customers, real orders and real problems show up.

This is a real change. Big technology companies were never supposed to work this way. The old model was clean — build a product once and sell it to everyone. When the world’s leading AI companies spend billions to put their own people inside customer businesses, they are admitting something important. The scarce thing is no longer the AI itself. It is people who can make AI work inside a real business.

The size of the spending makes the point. Read together, the moves of this one spring form a clear pattern: Deployment has become the main event in AI in 2026, with billions aimed at the same job. These leaders now believe value is created on the day a system starts working inside a business — and keeps working.

This change did not come from a theory. It came from three hard years of test projects. An AI test looks wonderful in a demonstration — the data is clean, the users are friendly, and the results are impressive. Then the system meets the real business, and it struggles.

Real business information is messy. The same customer appears three times under three slightly different names. Prices are out of date. Every department keeps its own version of the truth. An AI system cannot spot any of this. It trusts what it finds and acts on it, quickly and confidently. That is where most AI projects quietly die — not in the demonstration, but in the first months of real use.

The numbers back this up. Gartner predicts that through 2026, companies will give up on 60% of AI projects that are not built on data that is ready for AI — data that is accurate, current and agreed across the business. In the same research, 63% of companies said they either do not manage their data the way AI needs, or are not sure that they do.

Gartner also warns that more than 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear results and weak controls. The AI itself is not on that list of reasons. The problem is the ground it stands on — the data, the daily process and the basic rules around it. That ground is exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is sent in to fix.

I have led data and AI teams for years, and this matches what I have seen. Businesses did not learn that AI was weak. They learned that their own house was not ready for it. Deployment is the work of getting the house ready.

So where is this heading? Gartner expects that by the end of 2026, 40% of business software will come with built-in AI agents that handle specific tasks, up from less than 5% in 2025. By 2028, it predicts, at least 15% of everyday work decisions will be made by AI on its own.

If even part of that happens, the key question for a business changes. It will not be which AI you buy — AI will keep getting better and cheaper, whoever sells it. The question will be whether your business is ready. Is your information clean and agreed in one place? Do you have clear examples of what a good result looks like? Are the rules clear for what AI may do alone and what a person must approve?

There is a second shift inside this one. The team that works inside a business every day learns how it truly runs — where time is wasted, where mistakes happen and where money is made. That knowledge decides what gets bought next. This is why the labs moved so fast. The engineer inside the building is becoming the most important seat in AI, and no one wants a rival sitting in it.

For founders and smaller companies, this is good news. The old race rewarded whoever could spend the most on technology. The new one rewards whoever understands a customer’s real work the deepest. Many of the important AI companies of the next decade will not build models. They will make AI work, industry by industry and business by business.

New models will keep making headlines, and they deserve to. But the future of AI will not be settled in a laboratory. It will be settled in offices, warehouses, clinics and shops, by people doing the unglamorous work of making AI succeed in real life. That work is deployment. And deployment is the main event now.

For the past three years, the AI story was a race to build a better model. Every few months, a company released one that was faster, smarter and cheaper. In 2026, the story changed. The biggest AI announcements of the year were not new models at all. They were new companies built for one purpose — putting engineers inside other companies to make AI work there.

In May 2026, OpenAI launched a new company for this, backed by more than $4 billion. Its engineers move into a customer’s business, learn how the work really gets done and stay until the AI works in day-to-day use. Days earlier, Anthropic announced a similar company of its own, built for mid-sized businesses that do not have enough technical staff to do this work themselves.

These engineers have a name: forward-deployed engineers. The idea started at Palantir. Instead of selling software and wishing the customer luck, the engineer sits with the customer’s own team and connects the AI to the company’s real information and real way of working. They are not judged on advice or presentations. They are judged on one thing — whether the system still works when real customers, real orders and real problems show up.
